title: Republicans run from Trump on Iran ahead of midterms | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Republicans choosing to distance themselves from Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections was somewhat inevitable, given howhistorically unpopular the president is.

But the examples are piling up, and it’s notably happening in some pretty red territory.

Many of those running away from the president and policies like the Iran war are campaigning in territory that favored Trump by substantial margins — including by double digits in some areas.

The Iran war defections over the past week have been particularly notable.

Three of the big ones have come from one relatively small state: Iowa. Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks joined ina vote to limit Trump’s war powerslast week. And on Monday, their colleague Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is the GOP nominee for Senate, posted on X that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

Hinson’s defection came the same day that her fellow Midwestern Senate nominee, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers, released an ad similarly saying, “The war with Iran needs to end — and end quickly.” By Tuesday, GOP Wisconsin gubernatorial nomineeRep. Tom TiffanyandOhio Sen. Jon Hustedboth signaled much the same.

Their moves come asnew CNN pollingon Tuesday showed just 26% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the war — a number that has gradually gotten worse.

That four statewide candidates broke with Trump already this week says a lot. But so did the fact that two of the states involved were Iowa and Ohio, which Trump carried by 13 and 11 points in 2024, respectively.

(Trump won Nunn’s district by 5 points in 2024, and Miller-Meeks’ by 9.)

There has been a sense that Iowa’s Senate race might be in play because Trump’s tariffs have hit the state particularly hard, and because Democrats recruited well with state Sen. Josh Turek.

And sure enough, the day after Hinson broke with Trump over Iran, a Marist College poll showedTurek leading by 8 pointsamong registered voters — perhaps the most eyebrow-raising Senate poll to date, and one that suggests she has reason to be concerned.

But it’s not just Hinson who has felt compelled to distance herself somewhat from Trump despite running in an electorate that he won by double digits.

The Miami Herald reported Tuesday that Florida GOP gubernatorial nominee Rep. Byron Donalds, a loyal Trump ally, hadscrubbed numerous prominent referencesto the president from his updated campaign website. Donalds also recentlyexpressed “concerns”about Trump’s proposal to give every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November.

Donalds is running in a state Trump carried by 13 points.

And he’s not the only one who has made such changes to his website — despite running in deep-red territory. So too haveCalifornia Rep. Young Kim(Trump +12), congressional candidatesin Florida(Trump +11) andin Kentucky(Trump +15), andeven Kentucky Rep. Andy Barr, who is running for Senate in a state Trump won by a whopping 32 points.

Another notable development on this front over the past week: A couple of GOP incumbents in heavily Hispanic — and double-digit Trump — congressional districts distancing themselves from the president’s hardline immigration policies.

In Florida, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar told Trump in a direct-to-camera ad thatsome Hispanic voters “feel betrayed”by his immigration enforcement activities, saying they go “too far” by targeting those who hadn’t committed non-immigration crimes.

Asked about her ad last week, Trump said he did “disagree with her” but indicated he still backs her.Salazar said Sundaythat she spoke with Trump, who was “very receptive” to her warning.

And in Texas, Rep. Monica De La Cruz touted her work to free a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient who was being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The ad twicecited a “broken” immigration system.

Trump won Salazar’s district by 15 points and De La Cruz’s by 18 in 2024, when he did remarkably well among Hispanic voters for a Republican. But recent polls suggest that demographic has swung significantly back toward Democrats.

Many of these moves are relatively subtle, rather than full breaks from Trump.

Saying the Iran war needs to end isn’t the same as saying it was a mistake. The website changes are rather quiet — at least until reporters notice. And even in her immigration ad, Salazar speaks to Trump is if he’s just getting bad advice rather than delivering on the mass deportations that he repeatedly promised during the 2024 campaign.

But the fact that they feel the need to distance themselves in these ways — even in territory Trump won pretty easily in 2024 — speaks volumes about how they feel public opinion has shifted.

And they likely won’t be the last ones to do it. If anything, they might have just opened the floodgates for others who didn’t want to cross Trump but now might feel compelled to do so.

This story has been updated with additional developments.
